## Statement

Three trials are in play in any emulation and only one of them is usually named. There is the ideal trial that would answer the decision-maker's question, the target trial that the investigator specifies, and the emulation the data actually support. Specifying the target trial closely around the available data conceals the distance between the first two, and the paper reports a single estimate as though the chain were tight. What does not exist is a decomposition of the total discrepancy into its four transitions: from the ideal estimand to the feasible target estimand, from that to the identified observed-data functional, and from that to the estimator's output. Without one, a reader cannot tell whether a surprising result reflects estimation error or the fact that the question quietly changed at the first step.

## Why it is open

The first transition is a change of scientific question rather than a statistical error, so it has no sampling distribution and no obvious metric. Any measure of distance between estimands requires a common space in which to compare an intervention that was never implementable with one that was, and that space has to be constructed rather than estimated. The incentives also run the wrong way: making the drift explicit weakens the paper's claim without changing its number, so nothing but a reporting requirement would make anyone do it.

## What has been tried

::: {.table-scroll}

| Work | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| [Moreno-Betancur M, Wijesuriya R, Carlin JB. The ideal trial: defining causal estimands that balance relevance and feasibility in target trial emulations and actual randomized trials. Epidemiology 2026;37(2):153-162](https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000001933) | Distinguishes ideal, target and actual trials and argues that every discrepancy between them should be made explicit. It frames the problem and does not supply the decomposition. |
| [Hernán MA, Robins JM. Using big data to emulate a target trial when a randomized trial is not available. Am J Epidemiol 2016;183(8):758-764](https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwv254) | Establishes the target trial as the object to be specified, which is the middle term of the three and the only one the framework requires be written down. |
| [Ren Y, Jia Y, Liu L, et al. Design and implementation of observational studies emulating a target trial. JAMA Netw Open 2026;9(2):e2558262](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.58262) | Design guidance for the operational steps, acknowledging that the operational methods remain scenario dependent. |

:::

## Probable solution or research direction

Define an estimand lineage that records each transition as a formal change in population, treatment version, outcome definition or follow-up, and require it in the protocol so it is written before the estimate exists. Quantify estimand distance through differences in intervention support and in target-population composition, which are computable from the data at hand and do not require the ideal trial to be feasible. Report the lineage next to the estimate so a reader can see which step is carrying the assumption load.

## Verification

::: {.verification-trail}
**Verdict.** Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Emulations should separately document changes from the decision question to the operational causal estimand, the assumptions mapping that estimand to an observed-data functional, and estimation uncertainty. This lineage need not form an additive numerical decomposition when populations, interventions, outcomes, or scales differ.

**Dissent.** literature dissented (supported-with-caveat): The framing is now published rather than a preprint: the ideal-trial paper the entry cites as arXiv 2405.10026 appeared in Epidemiology in 2026, and the entry should cite the journal version. [...]

4 of the 4 independent auditors returned an opinion on this entry.

Literature and prior-art check
:   **open / supported-with-caveat.** The framing is now published rather than a preprint: the ideal-trial paper the entry cites as arXiv 2405.10026 appeared in Epidemiology in 2026, and the entry should cite the journal version. A 2026 American Journal of Epidemiology paper sets out the anatomy of a causal estimand for population health research, which is the vocabulary a lineage would be written in. Neither supplies the decomposition the entry asks for: a formal accounting that attributes total discrepancy across the four transitions, with a computable measure of estimand distance. The claim survives with its citation corrected and its neighbors named.
    Cites 10.1097/ede.0000000000001933: The peer-reviewed version of the framing the entry cites as a preprint. The entry's citation should move to this..
    Cites 10.1093/aje/kwag079: Decomposes a causal estimand into its parts, which is the representation an estimand lineage would build on..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens
:   **open / overstated.** A structured estimand lineage is a defensible reporting objective, but the proposed decomposition is not mathematically defined. The statement names four objects but enumerates only three transitions. Under valid identification, the observed-data functional equals the target causal estimand and is not a separate loss term. If identification assumptions fail, the resulting causal bias is generally not identified from the same data. Effects defined using different populations, interventions, outcomes, or scales also have no canonical additive distance. Differences in intervention support or population composition neither decompose nor necessarily bound the difference between effects without bridge and effect-heterogeneity assumptions. This is therefore an open reporting and formalization item, not a universally available decomposition whose absence prevents interpretation, and its asserted high severity is inflated.

Grok 4.5, recency lens
:   **open / supported.** Inverted prior: searched for a formal four-step discrepancy decomposition (ideal→target→identified functional→estimator) in TTE. Own prior_work (Moreno-Betancur arXiv:2405.10026) frames ideal/target/actual trials and urges explicit discrepancies but does not supply a quantitative decomposition of total discrepancy into scientific-target mismatch, mapping loss, and estimation error. Hernán–Robins 2016 and Hansford 2026 are design/guidance, not decomposition. Searches for estimand lineage, estimand distance, and four-transition decomposition in AJE/Epidemiology/IJE/Sim/BMJ/JAMA and arXiv 2024–2026 returned framing and reporting proposals (ICH E9(R1), TARGET) but no operational metric or software that separates those four transitions. Still open as stated.

GLM-5.2, third independent lens
:   **open / overstated.** The claim asserts that a decomposition 'does not exist,' which wears the language of impossibility. However, the reason given for it being open notes that the common space required for comparison 'has to be constructed rather than estimated,' implying that the decomposition is structurally possible but simply has not been developed or standardized in current practice. The claim is thus a statement about the current state of the field framed as an absolute.

Decision path
:   `R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2/4)`

:::

## How the evidence falls in time

42 papers in the reviewed corpus bear on this problem, published 2010 to 2026. Progress and a fresh assertion of openness land in the same year.

This problem is **recurrent**: three or more papers spanning at least eight years assert it independently. Sustained restatement by authors who mostly do not cite each other is the strongest evidence this reading can offer that a gap is real rather than one group's framing.

It is also being **closed in pieces**: partial results come from more than one paper in more than one year, each covering a different part.
